title: ArrayDeque: High-Performance Resizable Array Queue
summary: Why ArrayDeque is the gold-standard queue: circular array mechanics, zero node allocation overhead, and superior speed over LinkedList.
prerequisites: The Queue Contract & FIFO Buffer Processing
ArrayList vs LinkedList: Performance & CPU Caching
learningObjectives: Understand the circular array architecture of java.util.ArrayDeque
Trace head and tail pointer bitmask wrapping: (tail + 1) & (elements.length - 1)
Explain power-of-two capacity sizing and doubling expansion mechanics
Analyze why ArrayDeque outperforms LinkedList in cache locality and memory footprint
expectedOutcomes: Complete mastery of circular buffer pointer arithmetic in technical engineering interviews
Ability to architect zero-allocation queues for low-latency Java applications

activities.title: Practical Context: Rotary Turntable Conveyor Belt

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Rotary Turntable Conveyor Belt
analogy.story:
Imagine a circular luggage carousel at an airport. Luggage enters at the tail pointer, moves along the belt, and passengers pick it up at the head pointer. When the tail reaches the physical end of the track, the belt does not stop or build new track—it simply loops back seamlessly to slot 0.

Only if the entire carousel becomes 100% full (head meets tail) does airport maintenance pause to insert an entire outer ring of track, doubling capacity. Unlike a train with individual railcars (LinkedList) requiring uncoupling and coupling, the circular turntable is a single continuous ring of memory.
analogy.keyTakeaway: ArrayDeque uses a contiguous circular array with head and tail indices wrapping around via bitwise masking, delivering blistering speed with zero node allocations.

activities.title: ArrayDeque Architecture: Circular Arrays & Bitwise Pointer Wrapping

keyTakeaways: ArrayDeque is backed by a circular Object[] elements array with head and tail int pointers
Capacity is strictly maintained as a power of two (e.g. 16, 32, 64)
Pointer wrapping uses bitwise AND: (tail + 1) & (elements.length - 1) instead of expensive modulo division
ArrayDeque outperforms LinkedList across both Queue and Stack workloads due to contiguous CPU cache locality

activities.title: Simulating a Circular Array Queue in Pure Java
activities.description: Trace the circular buffer pointer wrapping algorithm to observe how indices cycle from capacity-1 back to 0.

steps.description: Simulate adding items: tail advances sequentially via (tail + 1) & mask.
Simulate polling items: head advances sequentially, freeing front slots.
Insert additional items: when tail reaches 7, (7 + 1) & 7 wraps tail cleanly back to 0.

questions.question: How does ArrayDeque wrap pointer indices around the circular buffer without using modulo division?
options: Using an if-statement: if (tail == length) tail = 0
questions.explanation: Because capacity is strictly a power of two, (elements.length - 1) acts as a bitmask, wrapping the pointer in 1 CPU instruction.

questions.question: Why does ArrayDeque generally outperform LinkedList for queue and stack operations?
options: Because LinkedList is deprecated in Java
Because ArrayDeque stores elements in a contiguous memory array with superior CPU cache locality and zero node allocation overhead
questions.explanation: LinkedList allocates a 24-byte Node object for every element added, causing cache misses and GC overhead. ArrayDeque uses flat arrays with optimal cache prefetching.

questions.question: What condition signals that an ArrayDeque's backing circular array is full and must resize?
questions.explanation: In a circular buffer, when tail advances to equal head, all slots in the array are occupied and the array must double its capacity.

questions.question: What happens if you attempt to insert null into an ArrayDeque?
options: It is placed at the head
questions.explanation: ArrayDeque explicitly prohibits null elements; calling addFirst(null) or offerLast(null) throws NullPointerException.

questions.question: Why should you virtually never use LinkedList as a Queue or Stack in modern Java?
questions.answer: LinkedList allocates a separate Node object for every single insertion. Each Node contains two 8-byte reference pointers (prev, next), an 8-byte value pointer, and an object header, consuming 24-32 bytes of heap per element. Furthermore, Node objects are scattered across heap memory, defeating CPU hardware prefetchers and causing severe cache misses. ArrayDeque stores references contiguously in a flat array, has zero per-element allocation overhead, and runs 2x-5x faster in real-world benchmarks.

questions.question: How does ArrayDeque handle resizing when head == tail?
questions.answer: When head meets tail, doubleCapacity() is triggered. A new array of double the size (newCap = oldCap << 1) is allocated. Elements from head to the end of the old array are copied to the beginning of the new array, and elements from 0 to head are copied immediately after. head is reset to 0 and tail is set to the old array length. This maintains contiguous logical ordering.

questions.question: Is ArrayDeque bounded or unbounded?
questions.answer: ArrayDeque is unbounded. While its internal backing array has a fixed capacity at any given moment, it automatically doubles whenever it fills up, bounded only by available JVM heap memory.

practiceProblems.title: Compute Wrapped Circular Index
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement nextIndex(int currentIndex, int capacity) using the power-of-two bitmask formula to calculate the next circular buffer index.

practiceProblems.title: Compute Preceding Circular Index
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement prevIndex(int currentIndex, int capacity) using bitwise masking to calculate the preceding circular buffer index (wrapping 0 to capacity - 1).

practiceProblems.title: Implement Fixed Circular Int Queue
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a simple FixedCircularQueue with capacity 4 supporting enqueue(int val) and dequeue() returning the oldest int, or -1 if empty.
hints: Update tail = (tail + 1) & 3 on enqueue and head = (head + 1) & 3 on dequeue.

practiceProblems.title: Build Deque Ingestion Buffer
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Write a method createQueueFromTokens(String[] tokens) that returns an ArrayDeque containing all non-null tokens in incoming order.
hints: ArrayDeque throws NullPointerException if null is passed to offer/add.

practiceProblems.title: Reverse Queue Elements Using Deque
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an ArrayDeque<Integer>, reverse its elements in-place using double-ended operations.
hints: Pushing to a stack reverses order.
